attribution-s1.title: Invented study: why did a classmate fail?
attribution-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether people explain a failure differently when it is their own than when it is a classmate's.

Participants

64 high school juniors (ages 16 and 17) at one school in Oregon took part with a parent's consent and their own assent.

Method

Students were randomly assigned to two groups of 32. In the self group, each student recalled a time they failed a test and rated the cause. In the classmate group, each student read a description of a classmate who failed a test and rated the cause. Both groups used two 1-to-7 scales: how much the failure was due to the person (effort, ability), and how much it was due to the situation (a hard test, little time, a bad day).

Results

On the person scale, the classmate group's mean was 5.4 and the self group's was 3.1. On the situation scale, the classmate group's mean was 3.0 and the self group's was 5.2.

Invented study for practice.

attribution-s2.title: Invented data: locus of control and hours studied

attitudes-s1.title: Festinger and Carlsmith: paid to call a boring task fun
attitudes-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers tested cognitive dissonance theory: when people say something they do not believe and have little outside reason for doing so, they may change their attitude to match what they said.

Participants

71 male students in an introductory psychology course at Stanford University, who were required to take part in research for the course. Results are reported for 60 (20 per group); the rest were set aside for reasons such as suspecting the purpose of the study.

Method

Each student spent an hour on dull tasks: turning pegs and filling trays with spools. Each student was then placed in one of three groups (the paper does not say how). In two groups, the experimenter asked the student to tell the next participant (actually a confederate) that the tasks were enjoyable, and paid either $1 or $20 for doing so. A control group was not asked. Afterward, an interviewer asked each student how enjoyable the tasks had been, on a scale from -5 (extremely dull) to +5 (extremely enjoyable). At the end, the experimenter explained the true purpose of the study, and paid students were asked to return the money.

Results

Mean enjoyment ratings were -0.45 in the control group, +1.35 in the $1 group and -0.05 in the $20 group. The $1 group rated the tasks as more enjoyable than the control group and the $20 group.

Discussion

A 2024 replication in 39 labs (about 4,900 participants), using a related method in which students wrote an essay for a view they disagreed with, found people did shift their attitude after writing a statement they disagreed with, but not the key difference between people who felt free to choose and people who did not. How dissonance works remains debated.

social-situations-s2.title: Milgram: obeying orders to shock a stranger
social-situations-s2.html:
Introduction

Stanley Milgram asked how far ordinary people would go in obeying an authority who told them to hurt another person.

Participants

40 men aged 20 to 50 from New Haven, Connecticut, and nearby towns, with a range of jobs, recruited by newspaper ad and mail and paid $4.50 for taking part.

Method

Each man was told the study was about the effect of punishment on learning and was assigned the role of "teacher." A "learner" (a confederate) was strapped into a chair in another room. The teacher was told to give a shock for each wrong answer, increasing by 15 volts each time on a panel from 15 to 450 volts. The learner never received real shocks; each teacher was given one mild sample shock of 45 volts so the setup seemed real. When the teacher hesitated, the experimenter, in a gray lab coat, used set prompts such as "The experiment requires that you continue." Obedience was the highest shock the teacher gave before refusing to go on.

Results

26 of the 40 men (65%) continued to the maximum 450 volts. Every man went to at least 300 volts. Many showed strong signs of stress, such as sweating, trembling and nervous laughter.

Discussion

Later variations found less obedience when the experimenter gave orders by phone or when other "teachers" refused. A 2009 partial replication by Jerry Burger, stopped at 150 volts for ethical reasons, found 70% willing to continue past that point. Researchers who later studied Milgram's archived records note that the prompts were not always given as scripted and that some participants doubted the shocks were real.

psychodynamic-humanistic-s2.title: Do scorers agree on inkblot responses?
psychodynamic-humanistic-s2.html:
Introduction

Projective tests are scored by trained clinicians. Researchers asked whether two clinicians scoring the same inkblot responses would give similar scores, and whether a person's score would be similar six weeks later.

Participants

60 adult volunteers (ages 20 to 64; 34 women, 26 men) recruited through a community health center in one US city. Each gave informed consent. Responses were stored under ID numbers, not names, so no one could be identified.

Method

Each participant described what they saw in 10 standard inkblot cards. Two trained clinicians, working separately, scored every set of responses for hostility on a scale from 0 (none) to 20 (very high). Six weeks later, the same participants did the test again and one clinician scored it.

Results

The two clinicians' hostility scores for the same responses showed only a weak to moderate positive correlation. Scores from the first and second sessions also showed a weak to moderate positive correlation.

Discussion

The researchers concluded that hostility scores from this test were not consistent enough to use alone when making decisions about a person.

Invented study for practice.

psychodynamic-humanistic-s3.title: Acceptance and admitting mistakes
psychodynamic-humanistic-s3.html: Researchers randomly assigned 80 college students to two conditions. After a hard puzzle, an experimenter said either "I appreciate you as a participant, whatever your score" (unconditional) or "I appreciate participants who score well" (conditional). Each student then checked their own answers and marked their mistakes. The graph shows the mean percentage of their actual mistakes that students marked.

social-cognitive-trait-s2.html: Researchers gave 10 high school seniors a personality inventory and recorded each student's grade point average (GPA). The scatterplot shows each student's conscientiousness score (0 to 50) and GPA.

social-cognitive-trait-s3.title: Practice feedback and self-efficacy
social-cognitive-trait-s3.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether early success on easy practice items raises self-efficacy and persistence on a hard task.

Participants

90 students in grades 7 and 8 at two public middle schools in one Texas school district. Parents gave written permission and each student agreed to take part. Students were told they could stop at any time.

Method

Students were randomly assigned to two groups. One group first solved 5 easy puzzles (success group); the other first solved 5 very hard puzzles (struggle group). All students then rated "How sure are you that you can solve the next puzzle?" from 1 (not at all sure) to 7 (completely sure) and worked on an unsolvable puzzle. Persistence was the number of minutes before a student gave up, up to 20.

Results

The success group rated their confidence higher (mean 5.6) than the struggle group (mean 3.9) and worked longer on the unsolvable puzzle (mean 14 minutes versus 9 minutes).

Invented study for practice.

motivation-s1.title: The Yerkes-Dodson relationship

motivation-s2.title: Plate size and how much people eat
motivation-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether an external cue, the size of the serving bowl, changes how much pasta people eat when they are equally hungry.

Participants

64 adult volunteers (ages 18 to 45) at a university in Ohio. All gave informed consent, had not eaten for three hours, and were told they could stop at any time. At the end they were told the true purpose of the study, which had been described as a taste test.

Method

Participants were randomly assigned to serve themselves pasta from either a large bowl or a small bowl, with the same total amount of pasta in each. The researchers weighed each plate before and after the meal to find how many grams each person ate. Participants also rated their hunger from 1 to 7 before and after.

Results

Participants in the large-bowl group ate more pasta (mean 410 grams) than those in the small-bowl group (mean 320 grams). Hunger ratings before the meal did not differ between groups, and both groups rated themselves equally full afterward.

Invented study for practice.

emotion-s2.title: Recognizing facial expressions across cultures
emotion-s2.html: Researchers showed 60 photos of posed facial expressions (six emotions) to 40 adults in each of two countries. emotion-s3.title: Does holding a pen in your teeth make cartoons funnier?
emotion-s3.html:
Introduction

An early, well-known study reported that people rated cartoons as funnier when they held a pen in their teeth, which forces a smile-like expression, than when they held it in their lips, which prevents smiling. This replication tested the same idea in a larger sample.

Participants

400 undergraduate students (ages 18 to 24) at three universities in the Netherlands and Germany. All gave informed consent. An institutional review board at each university approved the study.

Method

Students were randomly assigned to hold a pen either in their teeth (smile condition) or in their lips (no-smile condition). Without being told the purpose, they rated four cartoons from 0 (not at all funny) to 9 (very funny). At the end, each student was told the real purpose of the pen.

Results

The mean funniness rating was 4.6 in the smile condition and 4.5 in the no-smile condition. The difference was not statistically significant.

Invented study for practice.

It is equally strong across cultures

It disappears in people with an internal locus of control

whether the student had ever failed a test
the student's grade on the test

why.1: Past failure was used in the self condition but was not the measure.

Elena describes herself as "a musician, a big sister, a night owl, and not much of an athlete." Which concept do these statements describe?

A researcher gives 2,000 adults a list of 300 adjectives to rate about themselves. A statistical method shows that ratings of "talkative", "outgoing" and "energetic" rise and fall together, while "worried" and "tense" form another cluster. Which method did the researcher use to find the clusters?

A job applicant answers 120 true-or-false statements such as "I keep my desk organized" and "I finish what I start." Her answers are scored against norms from thousands of adults. What kind of assessment is this?
Sam always arrives early, keeps a detailed planner and double-checks his work. On which Big Five trait would he most likely score high?
Rina feels calm in most situations, rarely worries, and recovers quickly from setbacks. How would she most likely score on the Big Five trait of neuroticism?
options: High, because she has strong emotions
Low, because she is emotionally stable

items.q: A coach says, "You can't understand a player's performance by looking only at their personality. You have to see how their beliefs, their habits and the team they play on all affect each other." Which perspective on personality does the coach take?
A student with high self-esteem fails one chemistry quiz. Which outcome is most consistent with what self-esteem means?
options: She still feels worthwhile but doubts her chemistry skills for now
She believes she has no chance of passing any science course
She begins to see herself as a totally different kind of person now
She blames her poor score on the teacher's handwriting

items.q: Using the figure, which example shows the environment influencing a person factor?
options: A student practices the piano for an hour each day after school
A teacher's praise leads a student to expect she can learn piano
A student's belief in her ability leads her to practice more
A student who practices more is invited to join a band

items.q: According to the figure, why would a trait-only account of a shy student be incomplete?
options: Because traits are measured mainly with ambiguous projective tests
Because traits are unconscious wishes held back by defense mechanisms
Because her shyness shapes the settings she picks, which shape her in turn
Because shyness is caused by the environment rather than the person

items.q: A teen with low self-efficacy in math avoids hard problems, so she gets less practice, and her test scores stay low. In the figure, which two factors does this cycle connect most directly?
Which statement best describes the relationship in the scatterplot?
options: A strong negative correlation: higher conscientiousness goes with lower GPA
A strong positive correlation: higher conscientiousness goes with higher GPA
No correlation: the points are scattered randomly
A perfect correlation: each of the points sits on the trend line

items.q: A school leader concludes from these data that raising students' conscientiousness would raise their GPAs. What is the main problem with this conclusion?
options: The sample of 10 students is too small to show any pattern at all
The scatterplot shows a negative relationship
GPA is a grade, so it is not a true number that can be correlated
It is correlational; a third variable such as sleep could explain both

items.q: The five students with the lowest conscientiousness scores had GPAs of 2.4, 2.9, 2.6, 3.0 and 3.3. What is the median GPA of these five students?

mistakes.why: 2.6 is the middle of the list as written. Put the values in order first: 2.4, 2.6, 2.9, 3.0, 3.3.
That is the mean. The median is the middle value once the list is in order.

items.q: On the inventory's published norms, conscientiousness scores follow a normal curve with a mean of 30 and a standard deviation of 6. By the 68-95-99.7 rule, about what percent of people score below 36?

mistakes.why: 34% is only the slice between the mean and one standard deviation above it. Add the 50% below the mean.
68% lies within one standard deviation on both sides. The question asks for everything below 36.

items.q: Which research method did this study use?
Write the operational definition of persistence in this study.

specific.model: Persistence was measured as the number of minutes, up to 20, a student worked before giving up on the unsolvable puzzle.

opdef.label: Operational definition
options: the number of minutes, up to 20, before giving up

why.1: A feeling of determination is the concept, not how it was measured.
why.2: The 1 to 7 rating measured self-efficacy, the other dependent variable.

why.1: The practice puzzles were the manipulation; persistence was timed on the unsolvable puzzle.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the confidence results?
options: The struggle group was more confident, which shows failure builds self-efficacy
Both groups were equally confident, so practice made no difference
The success group was more confident, as social-cognitive theory predicts
The success group was more confident because they were naturally smarter

items.q: To which population can these results most reasonably be generalized?
options: Adults in the United States, because 90 students is a large sample for a study
US middle schoolers, since the participants were public school 7th and 8th graders
Students in many countries, because puzzles look much the same across cultures
No one, because the puzzle was unsolvable

items.q: Twins Ava and Bea score almost the same on extraversion. Ava becomes a teacher in a busy school; Bea works alone as a night-shift lab technician. Ten years later, Ava reports more confidence speaking in groups. Which conclusion best combines trait theory and social-cognitive theory?
options: Their traits match, so the difference likely comes from unconscious conflicts
Traits decide behavior, so the difference is probably a measurement error
Similar traits can lead to different self-efficacy in different environments
Extraversion is a learned habit that has little link to heredity

items.q: After a long run on a hot day, Tomas feels thirsty and drinks until the feeling goes away. Which theory of motivation best explains his behavior?
Liam has just eaten a large dinner and feels full, yet he orders dessert when he sees the cheesecake on the menu. Which theory best explains this choice?

A spider raised alone in a lab, which has never seen another spider build a web, spins the same complex web pattern as every other spider of its species on its first try. Which concept best explains this behavior?
Kenji goes skydiving on weekends, rides the fastest roller coasters, and gets bored with routine jobs. Which concept best describes him?
Ari plays guitar for hours because she loves how it feels to finally nail a hard song. Which kind of motivation is this?

A child loves drawing. Her parents start paying her a dollar for every drawing. Months later the payments stop, and she draws much less than she did before the payments began. Which concept best explains the drop?
Jada must choose between two colleges she loves equally: one near the beach and one with a great music program. Which kind of motivational conflict is this?
Omar wants to try out for the school play because he loves acting, but the idea of performing in front of the whole school terrifies him. Which kind of conflict is he facing?
Before lunch, a person's stomach releases a hormone that signals hunger to the brain. Which hormone is this?
Mice with a gene change that leaves them unable to make leptin eat far more than normal mice and become very heavy. What best explains this?
options: They make too much ghrelin, a hormone that signals fullness to the brain
Their external eating cues are stronger than other mice's
Without leptin, the brain never learns fat stores are full, so appetite stays high
Leptin increases appetite, so less leptin should cause weight loss

items.q: At a party, Mia keeps eating chips from a big bowl in front of her even though she ate dinner an hour ago. When the bowl is moved across the room, she stops. Which concept best explains her eating?
First-year students who join a club in their first month report less loneliness and are more likely to stay at the college. Which motive does this finding most directly illustrate?
According to the figure, what happens to performance as arousal rises from very low to very high?
options: It rises to a peak, then falls
It rises steadily the whole way
It falls steadily the whole way
It stays flat until arousal is high

items.q: A skilled typist and a beginner both take a typing test in a loud, high-pressure room. Based on the figure, who is more likely to perform worse than usual?
options: The skilled typist, because high arousal harms well-practiced tasks most
Neither, because arousal does not affect typing
The beginner, because for a new task performance drops at a lower level of arousal
Both equally, because their curves have the same shape and peak

items.q: A coach wants her team, who are experts at a simple drill, to perform it at their best. Using the figure, what level of arousal should she aim for?
options: As low as possible, so players stay fully relaxed
Fairly high, near the peak of the solid curve
As high as possible, because more arousal keeps helping
Low, near the peak of the dashed curve

items.q: Which concept does this study most directly test?
What was the dependent variable in this study?
options: Grams of pasta eaten, from weighing plates before and after
The size of the serving bowl, large or small
Three hours without eating before the study
The age range of participants, 18 to 45

items.q: Which ethical safeguard did the researchers use because they had told participants it was a taste test?
options: Confidentiality, by keeping names off the data sheets
Random assignment, by placing people in bowl groups by chance
Informed assent, by asking children to agree to take part
Debriefing, by telling them the true purpose at the end

items.q: Write the operational definition of how much people ate in this study.

specific.frame: Amount eaten was measured as ___, found by ___.
specific.model: Amount eaten was measured as the grams of pasta each person ate, found by weighing the plate before and after the meal.

opdef.label: Operational definition
options: the grams of pasta each person ate
the size of the serving bowl

why.1: Hunger was a separate 1 to 7 rating, not the amount eaten.
why.2: Bowl size was the independent variable, which the researchers manipulated.

how.label: Found by
options: weighing the plate before and after the meal
asking people to estimate how much they ate

why.1: The researchers weighed plates; they did not rely on estimates.

items.q: What is the mean number of minutes the expected-reward group spent drawing?

mistakes.why: 30 is the total for the group. Divide by the 5 children.
That is the unexpected-reward group's mean. Use the expected-reward row.

items.q: What is the range of minutes for the unexpected-reward group?

mistakes.why: 17 is the highest value. Subtract the lowest, 12.
That is the mean. The range is highest minus lowest.

items.q: Which conclusion do these data best support?
options: Any reward lowers children's later interest in drawing
Rewards raise interest, because the rewarded children drew more
The no-reward group drew least, so rewards are needed to keep interest
An expected reward, but not a surprise reward, lowered later drawing

items.q: Which concept best explains why the expected reward lowered drawing, while the surprise reward did not?
options: Drive-reduction, because the certificate lowered the children's drive to draw
The overjustification effect: drawing for a promised prize made it feel like work
Sensation seeking, because certificates are less exciting than drawing
An approach-avoidance conflict, because the children wanted and feared the certificate

items.q: Walking home at night, Nia hears footsteps behind her. Her heart races, and only then, noticing her pounding heart, does she realize she feels afraid. Which sequence of emotion does her experience fit?
options: The feeling of fear comes first and then causes the body to react
Body arousal comes first, and noticing it produces the feeling
Arousal and the feeling happen at the same time, neither causing the other
A display rule tells her which feeling is acceptable to show

items.q: A researcher argues that when a snake appears, the brain sends signals to the body (racing heart) and to the cortex (the feeling of fear) at the same moment. Which sequence is she describing?
options: A cognitive appraisal first, then arousal, then the conscious feeling
Arousal and the feeling occur together, neither causing the other
The feeling first, then a facial expression that matches it

items.q: Two students feel the same racing heart and sweaty palms before a concert. One thinks, "I'm so excited!" and the other thinks, "I'm terrified." Which idea best explains why they report different emotions?
options: The arousal is labeled by an appraisal of the situation
Arousal and feeling occur at the same time, so labels do not matter

items.q: A person sees a car swerve toward her, and before she can think, she jumps back and feels a jolt of fear. Later, she realizes it was a toy car. Which point does this support?
options: A conscious appraisal of the situation comes before each emotion felt
Arousal and appraisal are the same process
Some emotional reactions occur quickly, before conscious appraisal

items.q: Before a job interview, Rafi forces himself to smile and finds he feels a little more relaxed. Which concept does he believe explains this?

At a funeral in her community, Hana weeps loudly, as is expected there. In her new workplace abroad, she hides her sadness at a coworker's funeral because quiet grief is expected. Which concept explains the difference?

People from many cultures, including a remote group with little contact with outsiders, match photos of faces to stories about happiness, sadness and fear far more often than chance. What does this best support?
options: Display rules for showing emotion are much the same across cultures
Some facial expressions of emotion are widely recognized across cultures
Emotional expressions are learned mostly by watching television and film
The facial feedback hypothesis is strongly supported

items.q: After a day of laughing with friends, Tess finds she is more willing to try new activities and she makes a new friend. Over months, she builds lasting skills and relationships. Which theory explains this pattern?
Which part of the nervous system produces the racing heart, fast breathing and sweating that come with fear?
A patient with a spinal cord injury that reduces body feedback reports that his emotions feel less intense than before. Which sequence in the figure does this support most?
options: Sequence 1, since it says the feeling depends on noticing arousal
Sequence 2, because it says the body is the source of the feeling
Sequence 3, because it says there is no role for the body
No sequence, since body feedback is missing from each of the three

items.q: In an experiment, people given an arousing (but harmless) injection without being told its effects felt angry when a partner acted angry and happy when a partner acted silly. Which sequence does this best fit?
options: Sequence 1, because the arousal by itself produced one fixed emotion for everyone
Sequence 2, because arousal and feeling were simultaneous
Sequence 3, because people labeled the same arousal by the situation
No sequence, because the injection lowered arousal in these people

items.q: Which step appears in sequence 3 but not in sequence 1?
options: Body arousal such as a pounding heart
The event that starts the whole sequence
The emotion that results at the end

items.q: Which conclusion do these results best support?
options: People recognize emotions well in own-culture faces but not other-culture faces
Recognition was no better than guessing
People from the other culture showed no emotion in their photos
Expressions were recognized well above chance, but better in own-culture faces

items.q: By how many percentage points did recognition of own-culture faces exceed recognition of other-culture faces?

mistakes.why: 67 compares own-culture faces with chance. Compare own-culture with other-culture faces.
54 compares other-culture faces with chance. Compare the two face types.

items.q: A critic says the photos showed posed, exaggerated expressions. Why does this limit the conclusion?
options: Real-life expressions are subtler, so everyday recognition may be lower
Posed photos are not allowed in studies comparing two countries
Posed photos turn the study into an experiment instead of a survey design
Posed photos guarantee that recognition will be at chance

items.q: What do the results suggest about the facial feedback hypothesis in this study?
options: They strongly support it, because the smile group rated cartoons higher
They prove the hypothesis is false for people and expressions of any kind
They do not support it: the small difference may be due to chance
They show that holding a pen makes cartoons less funny for everyone

items.q: Which was the independent variable?
options: Where the pen was held: in the teeth or in the lips
The funniness rating each student gave, from 0 to 9
The four cartoons shown to each student
The three universities where students were tested

items.q: Which ethical safeguard does the summary describe, and how was it applied?
options: Random assignment, by placing students in conditions by chance
The right to withdraw, by letting students stop at any time
Debriefing, by revealing the pen's real purpose at the end

items.q: Why did the researchers not tell students the purpose of the pen until the end?
options: To keep the study's aim confidential from the universities taking part
To reduce demand characteristics, since knowing the aim could change ratings
Because informed consent is not required when a study repeats an earlier published one
To turn the study into a case study rather than an experiment

items.q: Write the operational definition of perceived funniness in this study.

specific.model: Funniness was measured as each student's rating from 0 (not at all funny) to 9 (very funny) for four cartoons.

why.1: Smiling was what the pen position manipulated, not the measure of funniness.
why.2: A general feeling is the concept, not how this study measured it.

why.1: The students rated four cartoons; there was no video.
